title: How will Mark Carney's appeal influence the Yorkton-Melville byelection?
summary: The Liberals are running Aaron Kienle, the sitting Mayor of Yorkton, as their candidate in the byelection set for Dec. 7.

image.caption: Yorkton-Melville Liberal candidate Aaron Kienle has received support during the campaign from Saskatchewan's only Liberal MP, Buckley Belanger. (Aaron Kienle/Facebook)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
The Liberals are running Aaron Kienle, the sitting Mayor of Yorkton, as their candidate in the byelection set for Dec. 7.
The true-blue riding has been held by Conservatives for more than 30 years
Opportunity.
Aaron Kienle, the sitting mayor of Yorkton, uses that word repeatedly as he talks about his decision to run for the Liberals in Yorkton-Melville.

If he's elected there's an opportunity to bring federal investment money to eastern Saskatchewan. Winning the seat would be an opportunity for Saskatchewan to have a seat at the table in the federal government.
The 44-year-old admits he had no membership in a federal political party even as recently two years ago.

Kienle says that since he was elected mayor of Yorkton in 2024 he's been able to meet and speak with members of Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal government, and those conversations convinced him Carney is interested in doing more for rural areas in the whole country.
The resignation of Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall presented the unique opportunity for Kienle to throw his hat in the ring in the Yorkton-Melville riding.
"There was no other party that I would ever consider. This is the one that's going to get the most done at this very crucial time," Kienle said in a recent interview.
An election sign for Aaron Kienle is displayed on a roadside in Yorkton, Saskatchewan on Nov. 20, 2026. (Laura Gillis/CBC)
The opportunity he repeatedly highlighted may have already become a reality.
In mid-October, the City of Yorkton received $74 million from the provincial and federal governments for a wastewater renewal project.
Yorkton received a further $5.6 million in federal money for housing construction.
Kienle was unveiled as the Liberal party's candidate at the end of October.
A historic break?
The weight of history is certainly against Kienle. Since 1993, Yorkton-Melville has sent a combination of Reform, Alliance and Conservative candidates to Ottawa.
Before that, it was part of the so-called "garlic curtain," a region in Saskatchewan that had high concentrations of Ukrainian and Eastern European immigrants and served as an NDP stronghold.
In short, the riding has never sent a Liberal MP to Ottawa.
Charles Smith, a professor of politics at the University of Saskatchewan, said rural Saskatchewan has some of the most conservative voters in the country.
"It would be surprising to me if we saw a swing away from that to win a seat for the Liberals or the NDP. Neither of those two parties have deep ground games in that area," Smith said.
"But I think you're seeing a confident Liberal Party and a kind of static Conservative Party."
One of the potential indicators of that confidence is that the Grits are now actively campaigning in Yorkton-Melville.
The only sitting Liberal MP in the province, Buckley Belanger, has been door knocking with Kienle. Former Liberal cabinet minister Ralph Goodale has also made an appearance.
Yorkton-Melville Liberal candidate Aaron Kienle has received support during the campaign from Saskatchewan's only Liberal MP, Buckley Belanger. (Aaron Kienle/Facebook)
All of this is happening in a riding where the last time a Liberal candidate got more than 15 per cent of the vote was in 1993, when Jim Walters earned 29.4 per cent.
In past general elections, the Liberal candidates have been staff members with a limited connection to the local riding.
In comparison, Kienle is a recently elected, seemingly-popular politician (he won the mayoral campaign in Yorkton with 62 per cent of the vote in 2024) with deep ties to the community.
"The Liberals clearly are trying to put their best foot forward," said Smith. "You certainly don't nominate the mayor of Yorkton with the hope of doing worse or losing."
Smith says byelections don't have the turnout of a general election and in many ways a party's ground game can make or break its fortunes.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's popularity looms large over the Yorkton-Melville byelection, according to one expert. (The Canadian Press/Justin Tang)

That's why the Liberals face an uphill battle, Smith said, although they will also be buoyed by Carney's popularity across Canada, even in staunchly conservative provinces like Alberta and Saskatchewan.
"[Carney's] more popular than Danielle Smith in Alberta. He's probably on par with Scott Moe, or close to it anyway," Smith said.
Pictured, from left, are the six candidates running in the Yorkton-Melville byelection: Aaron Kienle, Dionne Fehler, Nelson Pohl, Travis Patron, Valerie Brooks and Tammy Bobyk-Jacquemart. (CBC)
Byelection's crowded field
The Conservative Party is running farmer and small-business owner Nelson Pohl under its banner in the byelection.
Pohl's biography on the party's website highlights a hard work ethic and a belief that Canadians should be free to make their own choices.
Over the course of multiple weeks, CBC News has sent emails and messages to the Conservatives' national media team, the local Conservative electoral district association and Pohl's Facebook page.
No response has been received.
A Nelson Pohl campaign sign is displayed in Yorkton, Saskatchewan, on Nov. 20, 2026. (Laura Gillis/CBC)
Pohl will also be absent from an all-candidates forum hosted by the Yorkton Chamber of Commerce, scheduled for Nov. 24.
Kienle is set to attend, as are Green Party of Canada candidate Valerie Brooks and NDP candidate Tammy Bobyk-Jacquemart.
Dionne Fehler of the People's Party of Canada and Travis Patron, who is running as an independent, will round out the field of confirmed candidates in byelection, according to Elections Canada.
